title: Orbital Mechanics
tagline: The two-body problem, Kepler's equation, orbital elements, orbit determination, manoeuvres and transfers, rendezvous, interplanetary trajectories, perturbations and attitude dynamics
summary: Orbital mechanics describes how satellites and spacecraft move under gravity and how to change their orbits with as little propellant as possible. The course develops the two-body problem and conic orbits, position as a function of time, orbital elements and orbit determination, impulsive manoeuvres and transfers, relative motion and rendezvous, interplanetary trajectories, orbital perturbations, and the attitude dynamics and control of spacecraft.
overview: Orbital mechanics applies Newton's laws of motion and gravitation to artificial satellites and spacecraft. The course starts from the two-body problem: conservation of angular momentum and energy and the eccentricity vector lead to conic-section orbits and the vis-viva equation, and Kepler's equation gives the position on an orbit as a function of time. Orbital elements describe orbits in three dimensions, and the Gibbs and Lambert problems and least squares turn observations into orbits.

The middle of the course is about changing orbits. Impulsive manoeuvres are costed in delta-v: Hohmann and bi-elliptic transfers, plane changes and how to combine them, and phasing. The Clohessy–Wiltshire equations describe the motion of one spacecraft relative to another in a nearby circular orbit, and give the targeting burns for rendezvous. Patched conics join planet-centred hyperbolas to a heliocentric transfer to size interplanetary missions, and explain the gravity assist.

The last two chapters go beyond the ideal two-body problem. Gauss's variational equations show how small forces change the orbital elements: the Earth's oblateness (J2) turns the orbital plane and the line of apsides — the basis of sun-synchronous and Molniya orbits — while atmospheric drag shrinks low orbits and sets their lifetime. Euler's equations govern the spacecraft's orientation: spin stability and the major-axis rule, the gravity-gradient torque, and attitude control with reaction wheels, magnetic torquers and feedback.

Every chapter works with real numbers — Earth orbits, the Earth–Mars transfer, Jupiter flybys, space-station rendezvous — checked by computation, and uses interactive figures to show how the results depend on the parameters. The material underlies mission design, satellite operations and spacecraft guidance and control.
outcomes: Derive the conic-section orbit equation and the vis-viva equation from Newton's law of gravitation and the conservation of energy and angular momentum
Solve Kepler's equation for elliptic and hyperbolic orbits by Newton's method and find the time of flight between two positions
Convert between state vectors and classical orbital elements, and determine an orbit from three position vectors (Gibbs) or two positions and a time of flight (Lambert)
Calculate delta-v for Hohmann and bi-elliptic transfers, plane changes and phasing manoeuvres, and judge which transfer is cheaper
Use the Clohessy–Wiltshire equations to predict relative motion and to compute two-impulse rendezvous manoeuvres
Size interplanetary missions with patched conics: hyperbolic excess speeds, departure and capture burns, launch windows and gravity assists
Calculate J2 nodal regression and apsidal rotation, design sun-synchronous and critically inclined orbits, and estimate orbital lifetime under drag
Apply Euler's equations to torque-free motion, spin stability and gravity-gradient stabilisation, and size reaction-wheel slews and PD attitude controllers

chapters.title: The two-body problem
chapters.summary: Newton's law of gravitation, the equations of relative motion, the conserved energy and angular momentum, and conic-section orbits.

chapters.title: Orbital position as a function of time
chapters.summary: Kepler's laws, the anomalies, and Kepler's equation for elliptic, parabolic and hyperbolic orbits.

chapters.title: Orbits in three dimensions
chapters.summary: Reference frames, the classical orbital elements, and conversion between orbital elements and state vectors.

chapters.title: Orbit determination
chapters.summary: The Gibbs and Lambert problems, and determining an orbit from observations.

chapters.title: Orbital manoeuvres
chapters.summary: Impulsive manoeuvres, Hohmann and bi-elliptic transfers, plane changes and phasing manoeuvres.

chapters.title: Relative motion and rendezvous
chapters.summary: The Clohessy–Wiltshire equations, and rendezvous and docking manoeuvres.

chapters.title: Interplanetary trajectories
chapters.summary: Patched conics, spheres of influence, hyperbolic departure and arrival, and gravity assists.

chapters.title: Orbital perturbations
chapters.summary: The Earth's oblateness and the J2 effects, sun-synchronous and frozen orbits, atmospheric drag and third-body effects.

chapters.title: Spacecraft attitude dynamics and control
chapters.summary: Euler's equations for spacecraft, spin and gravity-gradient stabilisation, and attitude control with reaction wheels and thrusters.

history.title: Kepler's first two laws
history.detail: Johannes Kepler publishes Astronomia nova, in which the orbit of Mars is an ellipse with the Sun at a focus and the line from the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times; the third law, relating period and orbit size, follows in Harmonices mundi (1619).

history.title: Newton's Principia
history.detail: Isaac Newton publishes Philosophiae naturalis principia mathematica, deriving Kepler's laws from the laws of motion and the inverse-square law of gravitation.

history.title: Lambert's theorem
history.detail: Johann Heinrich Lambert shows that the time to travel between two points on a conic orbit depends only on the semi-major axis, the sum of the two radii and the chord between them — the basis of the problem now named after him.

history.title: Lagrange's three-body solutions
history.detail: Joseph-Louis Lagrange's prize essay on the three-body problem finds the equilibrium configurations now called the Lagrange points, later used as locations for space telescopes and solar observatories.

history.title: Gauss's Theoria motus
history.detail: Carl Friedrich Gauss publishes his methods of orbit determination, developed in 1801 to recover the asteroid Ceres from a few weeks of Giuseppe Piazzi's observations, together with the method of least squares.

history.title: Hohmann's transfer orbit
history.detail: Walter Hohmann's book Die Erreichbarkeit der Himmelskörper (The attainability of celestial bodies) analyses the minimum-energy two-impulse transfer between circular orbits.

history.title: Explorer 1 and the major-axis rule
history.detail: Explorer 1, spun about its long axis, begins to tumble soon after launch; Ronald Bracewell and Owen Garriott explain that energy dissipated in its flexible antennas drives the spin towards the axis of maximum moment of inertia.

history.title: Satellites measure the Earth's shape
history.detail: R. H. Merson and D. G. King-Hele derive the Earth's flattening from the rotation of the orbital plane of the Sputnik 2 rocket; in 1959 John O'Keefe, Ann Eckels and R. K. Squires find the odd harmonic J3 (the 'pear shape') from Vanguard 1.

history.title: The Clohessy–Wiltshire equations
history.detail: W. H. Clohessy and R. S. Wiltshire publish the linearised equations of relative motion for rendezvous with a target in circular orbit (equations equivalent to those of G. W. Hill's 1878 lunar theory).

history.title: First rendezvous in orbit
history.detail: Gemini 6A, flown by Walter Schirra and Thomas Stafford, rendezvouses with Gemini 7 on 15 December 1965, approaching to within about 30 cm.

history.title: First planetary gravity assist
history.detail: Mariner 10 flies past Venus on 5 February 1974 and uses its gravity to reach Mercury, the first use of a planetary flyby to reach another planet.

history.title: Voyager and the outer-planet alignment
history.detail: Voyager 2 (20 August) and Voyager 1 (5 September) are launched to use the alignment of the giant planets for a chain of gravity assists identified by Gary Flandro at JPL in the mid-1960s; Voyager 2 reaches Neptune in 1989.

history.title: JWST arrives at Sun–Earth L2
history.detail: The James Webb Space Telescope enters its orbit around the Sun–Earth L2 point on 24 January 2022, a month after launch.

references.title: Orbital Mechanics for Engineering Students (4th edition)
references.note: The closest match to this course: two-body problem, Kepler's equation, orbital elements, Gibbs and Lambert, manoeuvres, relative motion, interplanetary trajectories and attitude dynamics, with many worked examples.

references.authors: R. R. Bate, D. D. Mueller, J. E. White and W. W. Saylor
references.title: Fundamentals of Astrodynamics (2nd edition)
references.note: The classic inexpensive introduction (first edition 1971), strong on orbit determination, Lambert's problem and the universal-variable formulation.

references.title: Fundamentals of Astrodynamics and Applications (4th edition)
references.note: Comprehensive reference with algorithms for Kepler's equation, Lambert, coordinate frames, perturbations (including Gauss's equations and J2 effects) and atmospheric models.

references.authors: J. E. Prussing and B. A. Conway
references.title: Orbital Mechanics (2nd edition)
references.note: Concise graduate-level text: Lambert's problem, optimal impulsive transfers, Clohessy–Wiltshire equations, perturbations and gravity assists.

references.title: An Introduction to the Mathematics and Methods of Astrodynamics (revised edition)
references.note: The advanced reference for Lambert's problem, the variation of parameters and perturbation theory.

references.authors: H. Schaub and J. L. Junkins
references.title: Analytical Mechanics of Space Systems (4th edition)
references.note: Rigid-body kinematics and attitude representations, Euler's equations, attitude control, and relative orbital motion.

references.title: Space Vehicle Dynamics and Control (2nd edition)
references.note: Orbital and attitude dynamics with a control-engineering emphasis: spin stability, gravity gradient, reaction wheels and control-moment gyroscopes.

references.title: Satellite Orbits: Models, Methods and Applications
references.note: Force models, numerical integration and precise orbit determination as practised in satellite operations.

references.title: Theory of Orbits: The Restricted Problem of Three Bodies
references.note: The classic monograph on the restricted three-body problem, the Lagrange points and the Jacobi integral — the next step beyond patched conics.
